rv.q: This trio make the sharing of a bowl of olives look like a power game.
This play, which is 90 minutes straight through — a delightful length — isn’t about art as in the white square but the art of arguing (and the art of friendship).

The expert playing of the three actors here gives us intimations of the bleakness hovering round a story about the fear of change and of men reduced – via a ridiculous unravelling process – to puzzling over what they ever thought they had in common.
The writing crackles like young wood on a fire and the whole show is over in 90 minutes without an interval. My, I do love a succinct show.
It’s droll, clever and incisive, but slightly too smart for its own good.
What emerges from this revival is the sharp distinction between the three characters.
Reza, Warchus and the fine cast’s skill is to use absurdist humour to portray the midlife crisis in genuinely thoughtful light.
Art remains a funny and thought-provoking bit of theatre, bursting with ideas and sly aperçus.
Every positive word said about this amazing play is richly deserved. A wonderful show.
One wonders what those same onlookers might make of the current and very fine revival at the Old Vic Theater.
It might be the most brilliantly awful play ever written – and, worse, it’s one step ahead.
This terrific revival demonstrates that the play qualifies in both categories.
Key’s shaggy dog approach, resonant and eschewing brittleness steals this show.

cn.t: Critics find this 20-year revival of Reza's sharp comedy about friendship and a white painting mostly successful, praising Warchus's skilled direction and the cast's performances, though some question whether it still resonates today.
